Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette:
Kofi was a man who understood fabric. For years, his small tailor shop was his sanctuary, a place where the steady rhythm of the sewing machine and the precise geometry of a pattern brought order to the world. He was 33, single, and his craft was his pride. That all changed nine months ago, on a Tuesday he was at the central market sourcing new textiles. The first explosion was a sound he felt in his teeth. The second was chaos. He remembers the cloud of dust, the splintering wood of a vendor’s stall, and a searing, metallic smell. After that, there are only fragments.

His memory of the event is a tormenting and inconsistent thing. Most days, it plays in his head like a film on a loop: the initial blast, the screams, the sight of people running. This intrusive replay can be triggered by anything—a car backfiring, the clatter of a dropped bolt of fabric in his shop. When the film starts, his body responds instantly, as if the danger were present and real. He finds himself scanning for exits the moment he enters any room, a frantic accounting of escape routes. In his own shop, he has rearranged the entire layout so his chair is wedged into a corner, his back always against a wall, where he can see the door at all times. Yet at other times, when he tries to deliberately recall what happened, to make sense of the sequence, there are just gaps, black holes in the narrative. He can’t remember how he got out of the market or how he got home. This fractured recall has become a source of profound self-doubt; he feels he can’t trust his own mind, and by extension, can’t trust that he will do the right thing in a moment of crisis.

The memory of himself frozen behind a collapsed fruit stand has calcified into a core belief: he is a weak person. This conviction colours everything. He replays not just the event, but his own inaction, each viewing another piece of evidence for his fundamental inadequacy. This feeling of weakness is inseparable from the constant, exhausting sense of threat he now lives with. Being perpetually on guard, feeling unsafe even in his own home, has reinforced a devastating sense of alienation. He has come to believe he no longer belongs anywhere, a ghost haunting the edges of a world where other people feel secure. The world is for the strong, and he has proven he is not among them.

This constellation of beliefs—that he is weak, untrustworthy, and alone—drives him to seek escape. He has all but stopped making plans for the future; the act of looking ahead feels fraudulent for someone so broken. His days are now structured around avoidance. To silence the film in his head and the gnawing self-recrimination, he loses hours, sometimes entire nights, to the blue light of his phone, scrolling through social media or playing repetitive games until his eyes burn. The constant, draining hypervigilance is another engine for this escape; the only way to get a reprieve from scanning his environment is to shrink his world down to the four inches of a screen. When the digital distraction isn’t enough, he finds himself picking arguments with his family, creating small dramas that offer a sharp, immediate focus, a different kind of adrenaline that momentarily eclipses the deeper, colder fear.

The cycle has become relentless. An intrusive memory of the attack confirms his weakness, which makes the world feel more threatening. The heightened sense of threat makes him feel more isolated and defective, which in turn drives him further into the isolating cocoon of his phone or the destructive release of a manufactured conflict. His work, once his pride, now suffers. Deadlines are missed, stitches are uneven. A long-time client recently, and gently, told him she’d be taking her business elsewhere. It was this loss, the tangible evidence that he was losing the last part of himself he respected, that finally pushed him to seek help. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate fear: that the man he used to be was gone forever, and he didn’t know if he had the strength to find him again.
